messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Non-profit Worker
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 76

The rain falls hard on a night twenty-three years past, when he finally pulls over on the service road outside Lahore. He is forty-five, taking a solo trip to meet a contact for a community development grant. The engine dies near the edge of a gas station. He steps out to check the hood. The man behind him moves without warning. What follows is a blur of weight, pressure, and a cold detachment that later settles in his bones like lead. He remembers the smell of diesel and wet asphalt, the sound of his own breathing growing shallow, the way his hands curl into fists but do nothing. When it is over, he walks back to his car, starts it, and drives home. He locks every door. He tells no one. In the years that follow, the silence grows heavier. As a South Asian man raised with unspoken expectations of dignity and control, the assault feels like a fracture in his identity. He buries himself in work, then in the slow unraveling of his marriage. His wife asks questions he cannot answer; the distance between them widens until the divorce papers arrive without ceremony. He keeps the violation contained, treating it like a structural fault in a foundation—something to be walked around, never repaired. But it leaks through. He begins avoiding highways. He develops a habit of sitting with his back to the wall, eyes tracking every entrance. He stops sleeping through the night. His mind replays the sequence on loop, a rigid script he cannot edit, forcing his body to brace against ghosts that no longer occupy the room. The dark becomes a theater of repeated motion, of hands that are not his own, of a breath caught in a throat that no longer trusts itself. Now, at sixty-eight, he arrives at my office with the same careful posture. He works for a non-profit that supports displaced families navigating bureaucratic systems. His days are filled with the rhythmic paperwork of grants and case files, a structure that keeps the intrusive thoughts at bay long enough for him to eat, to walk, to sit in my chair. He moves through their files with practiced calm, translating forms, securing housing vouchers, speaking softly to women who remind him, uncomfortably, of the vulnerability he once felt. The irony does not escape him; he lends his steady hands to others while his own foundation remains cracked. Yet his life remains tightly warded. When he walks into my office, he still scans the corners before settling. He still checks the time on his phone, not out of impatience, but to confirm he has an exit. Last week, a patient’s husband raised his voice at a front desk, and he spent the rest of the day in his car, gripping the steering wheel, waiting for his pulse to fall. He describes the feeling as a wire pulled taut behind his ribs, snapping every time a car backfires or a door slams unexpectedly. He speaks in my sessions with a measured cadence, but his hands betray him—rubbing his forearms, folding and unfolding his wedding ring, though he hasn’t worn it in decades. He tells me about the dream he has almost nightly, where he is running through the same gas station lot, but the pavement turns to sand and his legs refuse to move. He wakes drenched, convinced the air itself is still heavy with the threat he left behind. He avoids grocery stores after 8 p.m. He no longer accepts invitations to stay late at the office, though the work matters to him. The non-profit building has become both a sanctuary and a reminder; the fluorescent lights, the low murmur of voices, the way strangers lean in to listen—all of it vibrates against a nervous system that learned, long ago, that safety is an illusion. He sits across from me now, watching the rain trace the window, his breathing shallow but deliberate, carrying the quiet weight of a man who has survived a violation and continues to survive the aftermath, one measured breath at a time.
